title: Tight Bounds for Schrodinger Potential Estimation in Unpaired Data Translation
claim: Empirical estimation error decays with sample size at a near-1/n rate, matching the theoretical bound up to logarithmic factors.
layout: 1 panel, log-log scatter with fitted curve, legend top-right
description: A single log-log plot with a light dashed grid. The x-axis is the number of sample points, running from about 250 to 15,000 with ticks at 10^3 and 10^4. The y-axis is mean KL divergence, with a single labeled tick at 10^-3. Seven blue circular markers with dark outlines show observed KL divergence at increasing sample sizes. A solid magenta curve labeled 0.01·log^3(n)/n declines across the plot and passes near most of the points. The points scatter around the curve: the largest values sit at the top left, and the last two points fall below or above the curve at the right. A legend in the upper right names the two series. The eye goes first to the magenta line and the downward trend of the blue points.
caption: Dependence of $\E \KL(\pi^*, \widehat\pi)$ on the sample size $n$ in the case of two-dimensional Gaussian marginals $\rho_0$ and $\rho_T$. The expected KL-divergence was estimated from 10 runs. The purple line was fitted with linear regression ($R^2 = 0.94$).
abstract: Modern methods of generative modelling and unpaired data translation based on SchrÃ¶dinger bridges and stochastic optimal control theory aim to transform an initial density to a target one in an optimal way. In the present paper, we assume that we only have access to i.i.d. samples from the initial and final distributions. This makes our setup suitable for both generative modelling and unpaired data translation. Relying on the stochastic optimal control approach, we choose an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process as the reference one and estimate the corresponding SchrÃ¶dinger potential. Introducing a risk function as the Kullback-Leibler divergence between couplings, we derive tight bounds on the generalization ability of an empirical risk minimizer over a class of SchrÃ¶dinger potentials, including Gaussian mixtures. Thanks to the mixing properties of the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, we almost achieve fast rates of convergence, up to some logarithmic factors, in favourable scenarios. We also illustrate the performance of the suggested approach with numerical experiments.
